cards.front:
'Permafrost' — ground that remains frozen for two or more consecutive years — is a major climate concern because, on melting, it releases:

(A) Carbon dioxide only
(B) Methane and carbon dioxide
(C) Nitric acid
(D) Sulphur dioxide
cards.back:
(B) Methane and carbon dioxide

Climate Change & Agreements — Permafrost (mostly in Siberia, Alaska, northern Canada) locks up ~1.5 trillion tonnes of carbon — twice as much as currently in the atmosphere. As it thaws, microbes decompose the organic matter, releasing CO₂ aerobically and methane (CH₄) anaerobically. Methane is ~25× stronger as a GHG than CO₂ over 100 years. This is a major 'positive feedback' — warming triggers release that causes more warming.

cards.front:
The 'albedo' of a surface measures its:

(A) Ability to conduct electricity
(B) Reflectivity of incoming sunlight
(C) Carbon storage capacity
(D) Biological productivity
cards.back:
(B) Reflectivity of incoming sunlight

Climate Change & Agreements — Albedo = fraction of incoming solar radiation reflected back to space (0 = pure absorber; 1 = perfect mirror). Fresh snow ~0.80; sea ice ~0.50-0.70; dark ocean ~0.06; forests ~0.10-0.15. When ice melts, darker ocean is exposed — lower albedo — more absorption — more warming. This 'ice-albedo feedback' is why the Arctic warms ~4× faster than the global average.

cards.front:
'Ocean acidification' is caused chiefly by:

(A) Oil spills from tankers
(B) Absorption of atmospheric CO₂ by seawater
(C) Dumping of plastic waste
(D) Run-off of agricultural fertilisers
cards.back:
(B) Absorption of atmospheric CO₂ by seawater

Climate Change & Agreements — CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid) — seawater has taken up roughly 25-30 % of human CO₂ emissions, lowering surface pH from 8.2 (pre-industrial) to ~8.1 today. Lower pH dissolves the calcium-carbonate shells of corals, pteropods and certain plankton. Fertiliser run-off causes eutrophication (oxygen depletion), a different problem. Plastic and oil are physical pollutants.

(A) A low-emission scenario
(B) A high-emission 'business as usual' scenario
(C) A mitigation policy pathway

cards.back:

AR6 (2021-22) replaced RCPs with the broader Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), combining emission pathways with socio-economic storylines.

cards.front:
Glacial retreat in the Hindu Kush-Himalaya region affects billions of downstream people chiefly through changes in:

(A) Atmospheric humidity
(B) Dry-season river flows
(C) Solar radiation intensity
(D) Bird migration patterns
cards.back:
(B) Dry-season river flows

Climate Change & Agreements — Himalayan and Karakoram glaciers feed the upper Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra — crucial for dry-season (post-monsoon, spring) flows that keep the rivers running when the monsoon is absent. As glaciers retreat, flows initially INCREASE (extra melt), then DECLINE as the ice mass shrinks — 'peak water' is expected mid-century in many basins. ~2 billion people across South Asia depend on these rivers.

cards.front:
A 'carbon sink' is defined as:

(A) A source that emits carbon into the atmosphere
(B) A natural or artificial reservoir that absorbs more carbon than it releases
(C) A basin where coal is mined
(D) A storage device for fossil fuels
cards.back:
(B) A natural or artificial reservoir that absorbs more carbon than it releases

Climate Change & Agreements — Carbon sink — a natural or engineered reservoir that absorbs more carbon than it emits — slowing climate change. The three largest natural sinks are oceans (25-30 % of human emissions), land vegetation / soils (~25 %), and the atmosphere (~50 %, the part that stays). 'Blue carbon' sinks are coastal (mangroves, seagrass, salt marshes). India's NDC under Paris includes creating an additional ~2.5-3 billion tonnes of CO₂-equivalent sink through forest / tree cover by 2030.

cards.front:
The term 'tipping point' in climate change refers to:

(A) The budget allocated to climate action
(B) A threshold beyond which change becomes self-sustaining
(C) The moment sea level exceeds high-tide mark
(D) The election date of a climate-sceptic government
cards.back:
(B) A threshold beyond which change becomes self-sustaining

Climate Change & Agreements — A tipping point is a critical threshold where small additional forcing pushes a climate subsystem into a new state that is hard or impossible to reverse. Documented examples — Amazon rainforest die-back, Greenland / West Antarctic ice-sheet collapse, Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation shutdown, boreal forest die-off, coral-reef collapse. IPCC AR6 (2021) raised concern that several tipping points may activate at warming levels as low as 1.5-2 °C.

cards.front:
The MAJOR cause of recent sea-level rise globally is:

(A) Increased rainfall on oceans
(B) Thermal expansion of seawater + melting of land-based ice (glaciers, Greenland, Antarctic)
(C) Earthquakes
(D) Tide variations
cards.back:
(B) Thermal expansion of seawater + melting of land-based ice (glaciers, Greenland, Antarctic)

Climate Change & Agreements — Two main drivers — (1) THERMAL EXPANSION (warmer water occupies more volume; ~40-50% historical contribution); (2) MELTING land-based ice (glaciers + Greenland + Antarctica; growing share post-1990). Sea ice melting (Arctic) does NOT raise sea level (already floating, displacing equivalent volume per Archimedes). Current rate ~3.6 mm/year, accelerating. Total since 1900: ~21-24 cm. IPCC AR6 SSP5-8.5 worst case: ~1.0 m by 2100. Bangladesh, Maldives, Sundarbans — most vulnerable.

cards.front:
'Ocean acidification' refers to the ocean becoming more:

(A) Alkaline
(B) Acidic — CO₂ dissolves in water → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; ocean pH dropping
(C) Salty
(D) Hot
cards.back:
(B) Acidic — CO₂ dissolves in water → H₂CO₃ → H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; ocean pH dropping

Climate Change & Agreements — Atmospheric CO₂ → dissolves in oceans → forms carbonic acid → releases H⁺ → lowers pH. Pre-industrial pH ~8.2 → current ~8.05 (a 30% increase in [H⁺] since pH is logarithmic). Threatens calcifying organisms — coral, shellfish, plankton — whose shells dissolve in lower-pH water. 'Other CO₂ problem' alongside warming. Ocean has absorbed ~30% of human CO₂ emissions, slowing atmospheric warming but accelerating acidification. Saturation states (Ω) for aragonite + calcite track this.

cards.front:
EL NIÑO refers to the:

(A) Cold-water phase of ENSO
(B) Warm-water phase of ENSO — abnormal warming of central + eastern equatorial Pacific that disrupts global weather
(C) Indian monsoon system
(D) Antarctic ice cycle
cards.back:
(B) Warm-water phase of ENSO — abnormal warming of central + eastern equatorial Pacific that disrupts global weather

Climate Change & Agreements — ENSO (El Niño-Southern Oscillation) has two phases. EL NIÑO ('the boy child' — Spanish, named by Peruvian fishermen who first noted it around Christmas) — Pacific trade winds weaken; warm water sloshes east; severe rainfall in S America, drought in Indonesia, Australia, India (often deficient monsoon). LA NIÑA (girl child) — opposite, intensified trade winds, cool central Pacific, often strong Indian monsoon. Cycle every 2-7 years. Modulated by climate change (debated whether becoming more frequent / extreme).

cards.front:
The 'Greenhouse Gas Protocol' classifies emissions into three scopes. Scope-3 emissions are:

(A) Direct emissions from owned sources
(B) All other indirect emissions across the value chain — supplier upstream + customer downstream
(C) Indirect emissions from purchased electricity only
(D) Natural emissions from forests
cards.back:
(B) All other indirect emissions across the value chain — supplier upstream + customer downstream

Climate Change & Agreements — GHG Protocol scopes — Scope 1: direct emissions (own boilers, vehicles, factories). Scope 2: indirect from purchased energy (electricity, heat, cooling). Scope 3: ALL OTHER indirect — purchased goods, business travel, employee commuting, USE of sold products, waste, distribution, investments. Scope 3 is often largest (~70-90% of corporate footprint) but hardest to measure. SEBI now mandates ESG disclosures for top-1000 listed Indian companies (BRSR — Business Responsibility & Sustainability Reporting from FY 2022-23).

cards.front:
CAMPA (Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority) collects funds for:

(A) Conservation of marine ecosystems only
(B) Compensatory afforestation when forest land is diverted for non-forestry use
(C) Wildlife protection only
(D) Climate change research

An 'invasive alien species' (IAS) is best defined as:

(A) Any plant or animal not native to a region
(B) A non-native species whose introduction causes economic or ecological harm
(C) A native species that becomes dominant
(D) Any genetically-modified organism

(A) A medicinal herb

Water Hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes) is also nicknamed:

(A) 'Bengal's Bane'
(B) 'Terror of Bengal'
(C) 'Mughal Weed'
(D) 'Devil's Daisy'
cards.back:

'Prosopis juliflora' — known in India as 'vilayati kikar' or 'angreji babool' — is an invasive species native to:

(A) Australia
(B) Mexico and Central America
(C) South Africa
(D) Madagascar
cards.back:

cards.front:
The most abundant greenhouse gas by mass in Earth's atmosphere — though it is also part of the natural water cycle — is:

(A) Carbon dioxide
(B) Water vapour
(C) Methane
(D) Nitrous oxide
cards.back:

Methane (from paddy, livestock, leaks) is ~25× stronger per molecule than CO₂.

The carbon cycle's main natural 'carbon sink' — which absorbs roughly a quarter of annual human CO₂ emissions — is the:

(A) Atmosphere
(B) Ocean
(C) Ice sheets
(D) Volcanic rocks

cards.front:
The process by which water evaporates from plant leaves into the atmosphere is called:

(A) Respiration
(B) Transpiration
(C) Condensation
(D) Precipitation
cards.back:

Respiration — cellular energy production releasing CO₂. Condensation and precipitation — parts of the physical water cycle, not plant processes.

Lightning converts atmospheric nitrogen to nitrogen oxides, which wash down with rain and enrich the soil. This natural process contributes to the:

(A) Phosphorus cycle
(B) Nitrogen cycle
(C) Carbon cycle

'Shifting cultivation' — locally called 'Jhum' in north-east India — is chiefly an issue because it causes:

cards.front:
'Afforestation' and 'Reforestation' differ in that:

(A) Only afforestation is allowed by the Forest Conservation Act
(B) Afforestation creates new forest where none existed recently; reforestation restores land that was forest
(C) They mean the same thing
(D) Reforestation uses only native species; afforestation uses only exotic species

(A) Methane (CH₄)
(B) Carbon dioxide (CO₂)
(C) Nitrous oxide (N₂O)
(D) Sulphur hexafluoride (SF₆)
cards.back:
(B) Carbon dioxide (CO₂)

Pollution & Land — CO₂ contributes ~76% of anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions (largest absolute contribution). Methane is ~16% but ~28× more potent per molecule over 100 years (GWP). N₂O is 6%, HFCs/PFCs/SF₆ make up the rest but with very high GWPs.

cards.front:
The primary pollutant responsible for ACID RAIN is:

(A) Carbon monoxide
(B) Sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
(C) Chlorofluorocarbons
(D) Ozone
cards.back:
(B) Sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen

Pollution & Land — SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ / H₂SO₄; NOₓ → HNO₃. These lower rain pH below 5.6. Major sources: coal-fired power plants, vehicles. CFCs destroy stratospheric ozone; ground-level ozone is a pollutant but not the cause of acid rain.

cards.front:
Match the INTERNATIONAL ENVIRONMENTAL TREATY with its PURPOSE. A. Montreal Protocol (1987). B. Kyoto Protocol (1997). C. Paris Agreement (2015). D. Ramsar Convention (1971). List-II: 1. Phase-out of ozone-depleting substances (CFCs). 2. Conservation of wetlands of international importance. 3. Legally binding emission-reduction targets for developed nations. 4. Global pact to limit warming to well below 2 °C, ideally 1.5 °C.

(A) A-1, B-3, C-4, D-2
(B) A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2
(C) A-1, B-4, C-3, D-2
(D) A-2, B-3, C-4, D-1
cards.back:
(A) A-1, B-3, C-4, D-2

Pollution & Land — Montreal — ozone layer (CFCs). Kyoto — binding on Annex-I countries only, 2008-2012 commitment period. Paris — nationally-determined contributions (NDCs), global stocktake every 5 years. Ramsar — wetlands, named after Ramsar (Iran) where it was signed.

cards.front:
BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand) is a measure of:

(A) Oxygen required by fish to breathe
(B) Oxygen consumed by microorganisms to decompose organic matter in water
(C) Oxygen released by aquatic plants in photosynthesis
(D) Oxygen dissolved in atmospheric air above water
cards.back:
(B) Oxygen consumed by microorganisms to decompose organic matter in water

Pollution & Land — BOD is the dissolved oxygen consumed by aerobic microorganisms breaking down organic matter, over a specified period (usually 5 days at 20 °C → BOD₅). HIGH BOD = HIGH organic pollution = LOW dissolved oxygen left for aquatic life. Sewage-polluted water typically shows BOD > 30 mg/L.

cards.front:
Consider the following about PM 2.5. 1. It refers to particulate matter 2.5 micrometres or smaller in aerodynamic diameter. 2. It can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. 3. Major sources include vehicle exhaust, construction dust, and biomass burning. 4. The WHO's revised (2021) annual guideline value is 5 µg/m³. Which are correct?

(A) 1 and 2 only
(B) 1, 2 and 3 only
(C) 1, 2, 3 and 4
(D) 2, 3 and 4 only
cards.back:
(C) 1, 2, 3 and 4

Pollution & Land — All four correct. PM 2.5 is a major culprit in the winter-smog crisis of Delhi-NCR. India's NAAQS annual limit is 40 µg/m³ — much higher than WHO's 5 µg/m³, and typical Delhi winters exceed 100 µg/m³.

cards.front:
EUTROPHICATION of a lake refers to:

(A) Nutrient enrichment causing algal blooms and oxygen depletion
(B) Accumulation of plastic waste
(C) Freezing over in winter
(D) Rise in water temperature due to industrial discharge
cards.back:
(A) Nutrient enrichment causing algal blooms and oxygen depletion

Pollution & Land — Excess nitrogen and phosphorus (from fertiliser runoff, sewage) fuel algal blooms; decomposing algae deplete dissolved oxygen → fish kills and dead zones. Remedy: reduce nutrient runoff, aerate water, biomanipulation.

cards.front:
'Eutrophication' of a water body refers to:

(A) Depletion of oxygen due to thermal pollution
(B) Excessive nutrient enrichment causing algal blooms
(C) Salinisation from agricultural runoff
(D) Plastic accumulation in rivers
cards.back:
(B) Excessive nutrient enrichment causing algal blooms

Pollution & Land — Eutrophication — large amounts of nitrates and phosphates (from sewage, detergents, fertiliser runoff) fuel rapid algal and plant growth. When the algae die, their decomposition by bacteria uses up dissolved oxygen, causing fish kills and 'dead zones'. Classic example — toxic cyanobacterial blooms in Lake Erie. The Baltic Sea and parts of the Gulf of Mexico also have seasonal dead zones.

cards.front:
BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand) is a measure of the amount of dissolved oxygen required by:

(A) Fish and aquatic plants for respiration
(B) Aerobic micro-organisms to decompose organic matter
(C) Aerobic algae during photosynthesis
(D) Chemical oxidation of minerals
cards.back:
(B) Aerobic micro-organisms to decompose organic matter

Pollution & Land — BOD — oxygen consumed by aerobic bacteria over 5 days at 20 °C while they break down organic pollutants (sewage, food waste). Clean rivers have BOD < 3 mg/L; heavily polluted ones may exceed 30 mg/L. COD (Chemical Oxygen Demand) oxidises everything oxidisable (organic + some inorganic) with strong chemicals and is always higher than BOD. High BOD → fish die.

cards.front:
The 'Namami Gange' programme, launched by the Government of India, is focused on:

(A) Bore-well recharge in Tamil Nadu
(B) Cleaning and conservation of the Ganga river
(C) Afforestation in the Himalayas
(D) Wetland protection in the Sundarbans
cards.back:
(B) Cleaning and conservation of the Ganga river

cards.front:
Minamata disease — serious neurological damage caused by long-term water pollution — is caused by which heavy metal?

(A) Lead
(B) Mercury
(C) Cadmium
(D) Arsenic
cards.back:
(B) Mercury

Pollution & Land — Minamata disease — documented in Minamata, Japan in the 1950s — was caused by methylmercury discharged into Minamata Bay by a chemical plant and biomagnified through the fish consumed by the local population. Symptoms — ataxia, loss of peripheral vision, muscle weakness, damage to the foetus. The Minamata Convention on Mercury (2013) is the global instrument that bans / phases-out mercury uses. Itai-itai disease (also Japan) — caused by cadmium pollution.

cards.front:
Widespread groundwater contamination by arsenic in India is especially severe in:

(A) Rajasthan and Gujarat
(B) West Bengal and Bihar
(C) Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh
(D) Punjab and Haryana
cards.back:
(B) West Bengal and Bihar

Pollution & Land — Arsenic contamination of shallow groundwater is a major health issue in the Bengal-Bihar Ganga basin, and also affects Jharkhand, UP, Assam, Manipur. It is released naturally from alluvial aquifer sediments. Long-term exposure causes skin lesions, peripheral neuropathy and cancer. Fluoride contamination is more severe in Rajasthan, Gujarat, AP and parts of TN. Punjab faces arsenic in patches and uranium in deeper aquifers.

cards.front:
The Ramsar Convention (1971) is an international treaty for the conservation of:

(A) Endangered primates
(B) Wetlands of international importance
(C) Marine mammals
(D) Transboundary rivers
cards.back:
(B) Wetlands of international importance

Pollution & Land — The Ramsar Convention (signed in Ramsar, Iran, 1971; in force 1975) protects wetlands of international importance. Sites listed under it are called 'Ramsar sites'. India has over 80 Ramsar sites, including Chilika Lake (Odisha), Keoladeo (Rajasthan), Loktak (Manipur) and the Sundarbans (West Bengal). Wetland services — flood regulation, aquifer recharge, fish nurseries, biodiversity.

cards.front:
Drinking-water with fluoride far above the safe limit of 1.5 mg/L causes which disease?

(A) Scurvy
(B) Fluorosis
(C) Goitre
(D) Beri-beri
cards.back:
(B) Fluorosis

Pollution & Land — Excess fluoride causes dental fluorosis (mottling of teeth) and, in severe chronic cases, skeletal fluorosis (bone deformities, joint pain). Severely affected states — Rajasthan, AP, TN, Gujarat, UP, MP. Scurvy is caused by vitamin-C deficiency; goitre by iodine deficiency; beri-beri by vitamin-B₁ (thiamine) deficiency. Small amounts of fluoride prevent tooth decay (hence its use in toothpaste). dental and skeletal.

cards.front:
The magnitude of an earthquake is measured using the:

(A) Beaufort scale
(B) Richter scale
(C) Mercalli scale (strictly)
(D) Celsius scale
cards.back:
(B) Richter scale

Renewable Energy & Disasters — Richter scale (Charles F. Richter, 1935) measures magnitude (energy released) — logarithmic: a 7.0 quake releases ~32 times more energy than a 6.0. Modern seismologists increasingly use 'moment magnitude' (Mw) for large quakes. Mercalli scale measures intensity (perceived shaking on the ground at a specific location), with 12 roman-numeral levels. Beaufort scale — wind speed (sailors).

(A) Hurricane
(B) Cyclone (same term)
(C) Typhoon
(D) Tornado
cards.back:

The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) of India is chaired by the:

(A) President
(B) Prime Minister
(C) Home Minister

The Indian Ocean tsunami of December 2004 was triggered by a powerful earthquake off the coast of:

(A) Japan
(B) Sumatra (Indonesia)
(C) Chile
(D) Philippines
cards.back:

Which region of India is most vulnerable to landslides?

(A) Coastal Tamil Nadu
(B) Himalayan foothills and Western Ghats
(C) Thar desert
(D) Deccan plateau
cards.back:
(B) Himalayan foothills and Western Ghats

cards.front:
'Seismic Zone V' on the Indian earthquake hazard map — the zone of highest risk — includes:

(A) Central MP and Deccan plateau
(B) Kashmir, NE India, parts of Gujarat (Kachchh)
(C) Tamil Nadu and Kerala coasts
(D) Entire Peninsular India

cards.front:
GRIHA — India's national green building rating system — was developed by:

(A) BIS and CPCB
(B) TERI in association with the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE)
(C) ISRO and IIT Delhi
(D) World Bank

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of a green building?

(A) Rainwater harvesting
(B) Use of locally-sourced materials
(C) Heavy reliance on imported PVC and aluminium
(D) Daylight harvesting + low-VOC paints
cards.back:
(C) Heavy reliance on imported PVC and aluminium

Renewable Energy & Disasters — Green buildings minimise embodied energy by AVOIDING long-haul / high-energy-intensive materials. Aluminium has very high embodied energy (~227 MJ/kg). PVC is petroleum-based with toxic additives (phthalates). Both are usually substituted with bamboo, timber, fly-ash bricks, ferrocement, recycled-content steel. Other green-building features — passive solar design, green roofs, solar PV/water, low-flow fixtures, greywater recycling, EV charging, native landscaping (xeriscaping).

cards.front:
The 'Urban Heat Island' effect, mitigated through green-building practices, refers to:

(A) Cooler temperatures in cities than rural areas
(B) Higher temperatures (typically 2-7 °C) in urbanised areas vs surrounding rural areas, due to dense built-up surfaces and reduced vegetation
(C) Volcanic activity beneath cities
(D) Elevated humidity in coastal cities
cards.back:
(B) Higher temperatures (typically 2-7 °C) in urbanised areas vs surrounding rural areas, due to dense built-up surfaces and reduced vegetation

Renewable Energy & Disasters — UHI — concrete, asphalt, dark roofs absorb solar radiation by day and re-radiate heat at night. Reduced tree cover → less evapotranspiration cooling. Anthropogenic heat (vehicles, AC exhausts) adds. Mitigation: cool roofs (high-albedo), green roofs, urban afforestation, shaded pavements, reflective paints (SRI > 78), permeable surfaces. Indian cities like Delhi, Hyderabad, Ahmedabad have begun adopting Heat Action Plans; Ahmedabad's HAP (2013) was India's first.

cards.front:
'Embodied energy' of a building material refers to:

(A) Energy released when the material burns
(B) Total energy used in extraction, processing, manufacture and transport of the material
(C) Operational energy of the building's HVAC
(D) Solar energy stored in the material
cards.back:
(B) Total energy used in extraction, processing, manufacture and transport of the material

Renewable Energy & Disasters — Embodied energy — 'cradle-to-site' or 'cradle-to-grave' energy footprint. Per kg approximate values: timber ~2 MJ; brick ~3 MJ; concrete ~1.1 MJ; steel ~25-32 MJ; aluminium ~227 MJ; carbon fibre ~286 MJ. Strategies to lower: use locally-sourced low-energy materials (mud, bamboo, fly-ash), recycle/reuse (recycled steel uses 75% less energy than virgin), choose materials with high durability so the embodied energy is amortised over a longer life.

cards.front:
The unit used for measuring the absorbed dose of ionising radiation in tissue is:

(A) Becquerel (Bq)
(B) Gray (Gy) for absorbed dose; Sievert (Sv) for biological-effect dose
(C) Curie (Ci)
(D) Roentgen (R)
cards.back:
(B) Gray (Gy) for absorbed dose; Sievert (Sv) for biological-effect dose

Renewable Energy & Disasters — Three different concepts: ACTIVITY of source — Becquerel (Bq, decays/sec), older unit Curie (1 Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq). ABSORBED dose — Gray (Gy, 1 J/kg of tissue). EQUIVALENT / EFFECTIVE dose (biological-effect adjusted) — Sievert (Sv) = Gy × radiation weighting factor (1 for X/γ/β, 20 for α). Annual background dose ~3 mSv globally; ~6 mSv near Kerala/Tamil Nadu monazite beaches. CT scan — ~10 mSv. Lethal dose for ~50% of humans — ~4-5 Sv (LD50/30).

Vitrification of high-level nuclear waste is the process of:

(B) Immobilising the waste in a stable borosilicate glass matrix for long-term storage
(C) Burning the waste at high temperature
(D) Re-enriching it for fuel
cards.back:
(B) Immobilising the waste in a stable borosilicate glass matrix for long-term storage

Renewable Energy & Disasters — Vitrification — HLW liquid is mixed with glass formers (silica, boron oxide, sodium oxide) and melted at ~1,150 °C, then cast into stainless steel canisters. The BIOLOGICAL DIVERSITY ACT, 2002 of India was enacted to give effect to the:

(A) WTO Agreement on Trade-Related IP Rights
(B) UN Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), Rio 1992

(D) Vienna Convention on Ozone Layer Protection

Laws & Organizations — Biological Diversity Act, 2002 — implements India's commitments under the UN CONVENTION ON BIOLOGICAL DIVERSITY (CBD, 1992 Rio Earth Summit). Three objectives of CBD: (1) conservation of biological diversity; (2) sustainable use of components; (3) FAIR + EQUITABLE SHARING of benefits arising from use of genetic resources. Three-tier structure in India: NATIONAL BIODIVERSITY AUTHORITY (NBA, Chennai), STATE BIODIVERSITY BOARDS, BIODIVERSITY MANAGEMENT COMMITTEES (BMCs) at panchayat level. Aims to prevent biopiracy (e.g., neem, turmeric patent disputes). Distractor 1 = TRIPS (separate). Distractor 3 = UNFCCC (climate). Distractor 4 = Vienna + Montreal (ozone).

cards.front:
The Himalayan glaciated region is sometimes called the:

(A) Fourth pole
(B) Third Pole — because of the largest store of frozen freshwater outside the polar regions
(C) Cryosphere south
(D) Equatorial pole
cards.back:
(B) Third Pole — because of the largest store of frozen freshwater outside the polar regions

Laws & Organizations — Third Pole — the Hindu Kush-Himalaya (HKH) region, containing the largest mass of glaciers + permafrost outside the Arctic + Antarctic. ~50,000 glaciers spread across 8 countries (Afghanistan, Pakistan, India, Nepal, Bhutan, China, Myanmar, Bangladesh). Source of 10 major Asian rivers — Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra, Yangtze, Yellow, Mekong, Salween, Irrawaddy, Tarim, Amu Darya — supporting ~2 billion people. ICIMOD (International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, HQ Kathmandu) — coordinates HKH research. Glaciers are retreating ~10-30 m/year on average, with high variability. NASA / ISRO observations confirm consistent mass loss since the 1970s.

cards.front:
GLOF — a major Himalayan hazard — stands for:

(A) Glacier Lake Origin Formation
(B) Glacial Lake Outburst Flood — sudden release of water from a glacier-dammed or moraine-dammed lake
(C) Global Land Ocean Fusion
(D) Glacier Loss Of Form
cards.back:
(B) Glacial Lake Outburst Flood — sudden release of water from a glacier-dammed or moraine-dammed lake

Laws & Organizations — GLOF — Glacial Lake Outburst Flood. Climate-warming melts glaciers → meltwater accumulates behind moraine (debris) dams; the dam fails → catastrophic downstream flood. Examples affecting India: KEDARNATH FLOODS, June 2013 — Chorabari Glacier moraine breach + cloudburst → ~6,000 deaths in Uttarakhand. South Lhonak Lake GLOF, Sikkim, October 2023 — wiped out the Teesta-III hydropower dam at Chungthang and ~50+ villages downstream; ~100 deaths. SIKKIM, NEPAL, BHUTAN — many vulnerable lakes (Imja Tsho, Tsho Rolpa, Lemthang Tsho). NDMA + ICIMOD + ISRO are mapping high-risk lakes. Mitigation: controlled siphoning of lake water (Imja, Nepal — pilot project completed 2016).

cards.front:
According to the IPCC and recent ICIMOD reports, Himalayan glaciers are projected to lose what fraction of their mass by 2100 (under high-emission scenarios)?

(A) 10%
(B) Up to 80% (for the eastern Himalayas under SSP5-8.5; ~50% even under low-emission scenarios)
(C) 5%
(D) Glaciers will grow
cards.back:
(B) Up to 80% (for the eastern Himalayas under SSP5-8.5; ~50% even under low-emission scenarios)

Laws & Organizations — ICIMOD's 'Hindu Kush Himalaya Assessment Report 2019' and the 'Water, Ice, Society and Ecosystems' report 2023: under SSP5-8.5 (high-emission scenario), HKH glaciers could lose up to ~75-80% of their volume by 2100. Even at +1.5 °C (Paris Agreement target), losses ~36%. Eastern Himalayas (Bhutan, Nepal east) most vulnerable; Karakoram has shown some 'Karakoram anomaly' (slight stability or even mass gain) but is now also retreating. Implications: short-term flooding risk (GLOFs, peak flow), long-term DECLINE in dry-season river flow (Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra basin water security). Aerosols + black-carbon deposition from Indo-Gangetic Plain pollution accelerates glacier melt.

Laws & Organizations — CRZ-I covers ecologically sensitive areas — mangroves, coral reefs, turtle nesting grounds, salt marshes — and the inter-tidal zone itself. Development is virtually banned. CRZ-IV is the water area from the low-tide line up to 12 nautical miles out. The CRZ notification is issued under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.

cards.front:
The principle 'polluter pays' was incorporated into Indian environmental jurisprudence by the Supreme Court in which landmark case?

(A) Olga Tellis vs Bombay Municipal Corporation
(B) Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action vs Union of India
(C) Vishaka vs State of Rajasthan
(D) Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum vs Union of India
cards.back:
(B) Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action vs Union of India

Laws & Organizations — Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action vs UoI (1996) — the Bichhri tank case — applied the 'polluter pays' principle, holding H Acid Plant chemical firms strictly liable for damage caused by their effluents. The Vellore Citizens case (also 1996) further developed the precautionary principle. Olga Tellis (1985) was on pavement dwellers' right to life. Vishaka (1997) laid down workplace sexual-harassment guidelines.

cards.front:
An Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) in India is required before approving:

(A) Any commercial activity
(B) Specified development projects listed in the EIA Notification schedules
(C) Only foreign-funded projects
(D) Projects only above ₹500 crore
cards.back:
(B) Specified development projects listed in the EIA Notification schedules

Laws & Organizations — EIA Notification 2006 (most recent major revision; a draft 2020 notification is still pending) lists projects in two categories: Category A (central government clearance) and Category B (state-level). Trigger examples — thermal plants > 50 MW, mines above 5 ha, highways, airports, ports, industrial estates > 500 ha. Below-threshold projects don't need EIA. Public hearing is one stage of the process; the Expert Appraisal Committee recommends approval.

cards.front:
The Forest Rights Act, 2006 recognises the rights of forest-dwelling Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers over forest resources. The Act also gives the Gram Sabha which key power?

(A) Levy property tax on forest dwellers
(B) Consent over diversion of forest land for non-forest projects
(C) Appoint forest officers directly
(D) Override Supreme Court orders on forests
cards.back:
(B) Consent over diversion of forest land for non-forest projects

Laws & Organizations — Under the Forest Rights Act (FRA) 2006, the Gram Sabha is the authority that initiates recognition of individual and community forest rights. Its consent is required for any diversion of forest land for non-forest purposes in Scheduled V areas (upheld in Niyamgiri / Vedanta case, 2013). This is distinct from PESA 1996, which gives Gram Sabhas in Fifth-Schedule areas broader planning powers. FRA's implementing ministry is Tribal Affairs, not Environment.

cards.front:
The 'Extended Producer Responsibility' (EPR) concept has been incorporated into Indian rules covering:

(A) Drinking water quality
(B) Plastic, e-waste and battery waste management
(C) Air pollution
(D) Noise pollution
cards.back:
(B) Plastic, e-waste and battery waste management

Laws & Organizations — EPR makes the producer responsible for the end-of-life management of their product's packaging or waste. India has EPR under — Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 (amended 2022), E-Waste Management Rules 2022, Battery Waste Management Rules 2022. Producers must register with CPCB and meet annual collection / recycling targets. Extended producer responsibility is a polluter-pays variant aimed at incentivising better product design.

cards.front:
The UN Environment Programme (UNEP) has its headquarters in:

(A) New York
(B) Nairobi
(C) Geneva
(D) Paris
cards.back:
(B) Nairobi

Laws & Organizations — UNEP — established after the 1972 Stockholm Conference — is HQed in Nairobi, Kenya, making it the first UN agency based in a developing country. Leads climate, biodiversity and pollution agendas; convenes the UN Environment Assembly (UNEA) every two years. Inger Andersen (Denmark) has been Executive Director since 2019.

cards.front:
CITES (Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species) was signed in 1973 and entered into force in:

(A) 1972
(B) 1975
(C) 1985
(D) 1992
cards.back:
(B) 1975

Laws & Organizations — CITES — signed 3 March 1973 in Washington DC (hence sometimes called the Washington Convention), came into force 1 July 1975. Classifies species into three Appendices — I (prohibition of commercial trade, e.g., tiger, elephant, rhino), II (regulated trade), III (regulated unilaterally by one country). India is a member since 1976. 3 March is observed as World Wildlife Day.

cards.front:
The well-known panda logo belongs to the organisation:

(A) Greenpeace
(B) WWF (World Wide Fund for Nature)
(C) IUCN
(D) CITES
cards.back:
(B) WWF (World Wide Fund for Nature)

Laws & Organizations — WWF was founded in 1961 (Switzerland) and adopted the giant panda Chi-Chi (at London Zoo) as its logo. Works on biodiversity, climate, freshwater, oceans, food. Named originally World Wildlife Fund; renamed World Wide Fund for Nature in most countries in 1986 (US + Canada kept the older name). Greenpeace was founded in 1971 (Vancouver) around anti-nuclear-testing protests.

cards.front:
The 'Global Environment Facility' (GEF), which funds environmental projects in developing countries, was established in:

(A) 1972
(B) 1991
(C) 2000
(D) 2015
cards.back:
(B) 1991

Laws & Organizations — GEF — established 1991 in advance of the Rio Earth Summit (1992) — pools funds from donor countries to support projects on climate, biodiversity, land degradation, international waters, persistent pollutants. Hosted by the World Bank but operationally independent. Complements the Adaptation Fund (under UNFCCC) and the Green Climate Fund (2010).

cards.front:
'Silent Spring', the 1962 book that spurred the modern environmental movement, was written by:

(A) Wangari Maathai
(B) Rachel Carson
(C) Aldo Leopold
(D) Greta Thunberg
cards.back:
(B) Rachel Carson

Laws & Organizations — Rachel Carson (American marine biologist / conservationist) wrote 'Silent Spring' (1962), exposing the dangers of DDT and other pesticides — especially their biomagnification up the food chain into fish-eating birds. Triggered the US ban on DDT (1972) and the founding of the EPA. Wangari Maathai — Kenyan, founded the Green Belt Movement, Nobel Peace 2004. Aldo Leopold — 'A Sand County Almanac'. Greta Thunberg — Swedish youth climate activist.
